Voll literally means full like an object or container.  Do not use voll to mean full from eating. Use satt instead.  Crucially, saying "Ich bin voll" after a meal can colloquially mean "I am drunk," so using satt is the correct choice for food.

It is highly flexible and can modify adjectives, verbs, or entire sentences. It is placed either directly before the word it emphasizes or right after the conjugated verb in the sentence

1. Modifying Adjectives
When intensifying an adjective, besonders sits directly in front of it.
Das Wetter ist heute besonders schön. (The weather is especially beautiful today.)

2. Modifying Verbs (Standard Word Order)When modifying a verb, it usually sits right after the conjugated verb in a main clause.
Ich mag Schokolade besonders. (I like chocolate especially / a lot.)

3. Emphasizing a Specific Noun or Object
You can place it right before the specific noun phrase you want to highlight.
Ich mag Schokolade, besonders dunkle Schokolade. (I like chocolate, especially dark chocolate.)

4. Modifying Subordinate Clauses
When used with a conjunction like wenn (if/when) or dass (that), it modifies the whole dependent clause and goes right before the conjunction.
Ich trage eine Jacke, besonders wenn es kalt ist. (I wear a jacket, especially when it is cold.)

Key Syntax Rules to Remember
No Declension: As an adverb, it is invariable and never gets an adjective ending (e.g., never say besonderes Wetter).
Sentence Position: In a standard main clause, it fits perfectly into the "Middle Field" (Mittelfeld), after the subject and the verb.

As adverb ->  really, truly, typically

When echt acts as an adverb, it modifies verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. It does not change form. It is often used to mean "really" or "very" in informal conversation. 

Intensifier Example: "Das ist echt schwer." (That is really heavy.)
Verbal Modifier: "Er rennt echt schnell." (He runs really fast.)
Colloquial Question: "Meinst du das echt?" (Do you really mean that?)

As adjective -> real, genuine, authentic. Used to describe a noun and must be declined based on case gender, and number. 

 "Das ist echtes Leder." (That is real leather.)
Das Wetter ist heute ziemlich kalt.   (The weather is quite cold today.)

As a Conjunction (But/However):
Structure: Main Clause + , aber + Main Clause (Subject + Verb...).
Word Order: Does not change the word order. The subject remains before the verb in the second clause.
Example: Er ist nett, aber ein bisschen schüchtern (He is nice, but a little shy).

Can be used as a modal Particle (really/rather)

Aber can add emphasis, emotion, or surprise within a sentence, often translating to "really" or "rather".
Example: Das ist aber schön! (That is really nice!).
Example: Das ist aber teuer! (That is rather expensive!).

Acting as a coordinating conjunction that connects words, phrases, or independent clauses without changing word order. It functions similarly to English, placing items in a list (without a preceding comma) or joining two main sentences (e.g., "Ich esse Pizza und trinke Cola")
As a Conjunction ("or"): Connects alternatives, e.g., "Wir gehen ins Kino oder ins Theater" (We are going to the cinema or the theater).
As a Question Tag ("right?", "no?"): Added to the end of a statement to ask for agreement, e.g., "Das ist teuer, oder?" (That is expensive, right?).
As a Warning/Option ("or else"): "Lern, oder du fällst durch" (Study, or you will fail).
"Entweder ... oder": Means "either ... or," used for strict choices.
"Oder so": Means "or so," "roughly," or "something like that"

Standard Usage (Important/Essential):
Das ist sehr wichtig. (That is very important.)
Es ist wichtig, gesund zu essen. (It is important to eat healthily.)

As a Noun (Something important):
Etwas Wichtiges. (Something important.)
Alles Wichtige. (Everything of importance.)
Das Wichtigste zuerst. (The most important thing first.)

Comparison:
Wichtig (Important) 
 Wichtiger (More important) 
 Am wichtigsten (Most important)

It connects sentences or clauses in sequence, often appearing at the start of a sentence followed by the conjugated verb, though it can also appear later in the clause. It can also mean "according to it" or "for it".

Temporal Sequence ("After that/then"): Use to describe a chronological sequence of events, often interchangeable with dann or anschließend.
Example: "Ich esse zu Abend, danach sehe ich fern." (I have dinner, after that I watch TV.)

As an Adverb in Position 1: Frequently used at the beginning of a sentence followed by the verb.
Example: "Zuerst arbeite ich. Danach mache ich Sport." (First I work. Then I do sports.)

With Prepositional Verbs ("After it/that"): Used with verbs that require "nach" (e.g., fragen nach - to ask for/about).
Example: "Was kostet das? Ich frage danach." (What does that cost? I am asking [about] that.)

Weil is a subordinating conjunction in German that introduces a reason, requiring the conjugated verb to move to the very end of the clause. It connects a dependent clause to a main clause, always preceded by a comma (e.g., 

Ich bleibe zu Hause, weil ich krank bin - I am staying home because I am sick)

Sie konnten nicht mehr arbeiten, weil sie total erschöpft waren.(They weren't able to work anymore because they were totally exhausted.)

It is used for time ending (e.g., die Zeit ist vorbei - the time is over), physical movement past something (e.g., am Haus vorbei - past the house), or to express missing a target (e.g., daneben/vorbei - missed)

1. "Over" or "Finished" (Time/Events) 
Vorbei indicates that an event, period, or situation has concluded. 

Die Party ist vorbei. (The party is over.)
Der Sommer ist vorbei. (The summer is over/gone.)
Es ist vorbei. (It is over/It's all over.)

2. "Past" or "By" (Physical Movement)
It is used in conjunction with verbs of motion (often in prepositional phrases using an... vorbei) to describe passing something. 
Ich bin am Haus vorbei gegangen. (I walked past the house.)
Der Zug ist vorbei. (The train has gone by.)
Komm vorbei! (Come by! / Stop by! - inviting someone over)

3. "Missed" (Target)
Used when a projectile or action fails to hit a target. 
Der Schuss ging vorbei. (The shot missed.)
Vorbei! (Missed! / Past! - informal)

Ehrlich describes an action, a person, or an attitude of openness and lack of deceit (being honest), whereas wahr describes a factual state, statement, or reality that corresponds to the facts (being true)

It is used to describe trustworthy people, truthful statements, or genuine intentions. 
As an adjective (Honest/Sincere):
Er ist ein ehrlicher Mann. (He is an honest man.)
Sei ehrlich mit mir. (Be honest with me.)
Ehrliche Arbeit. (Honest work.)

As an adverb (Honestly/Really):
Ehrlich gesagt, das wusste ich nicht. (Honestly speaking, I didn't know that.)
Ganz ehrlich? (Quite honestly? / Honestly?)
Ich dachte wirklich/ehrlich... (I really/honestly thought...)

Key Phrases with "Ehrlich":
ehrlich gesagt (honestly, to be honest)
um ehrlich zu sein (to be honest)
ehrlich währt am längsten (proverb: honesty is the best policy)
es ehrlich mit jemandem meinen (to have honest/good intentions towards someone)

used for physical paths (straight), communication (outright/blunt), and time (immediately). It acts as a synonym for unmittelbar (immediate) but is more commonly used in everyday conversation to mean straight-on or straightforward

Key Usage Examples
Spatial (Straight/Direct): "Der Bus fährt direkt zum Bahnhof" (The bus goes straight/directly to the station).
Proximity (Right by): "Ich wohne direkt neben dem Bahnhof" (I live directly/right next to the station).
Communication (Blunt/Outright): "Ich habe es ihm direkt gesagt" (I told him straight to his face/outright).
Time (Immediately/Right away): "Ich komme direkt nach der Arbeit" (I'll come directly/right after work).
Frequency/Adverbial: "Er kam direkt auf mich zu" (He came straight toward me)

rules.rule:
Können is a model verb that expresses a possibility, permission, obligation or ability. It is always accompanied by a second verb in infinitive form which is placed at the end of the clause.

Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?  (Can I pay by card?)

Können is a model verb so you normally use the Präteritum(e.g. Konnten). The main verb is in the infinitive (e.g. sagen) and placed at the end of the sentence.

Wir konnten gestern leider nicht zum Unterricht kommen. (Unfortunately, we were not able to come to class yesterday.)

Passiv - Used to create passive voice. The Passiv is formed with a form of werden and the past participle. The past participle is always at the end of the sentence.

Der Blinde wird geführt. The blind (man) is being guided.

Die Brücke wurde nach dem Krieg gebaut. The bridge was built after the war.

Konjuntiv II - simple_past('Präteritum'), a verb form used to express hypothetical situations, wishes, unreal conditions, and polite requests. It roughly corresponds to the English "would/could" or "if I were..." structures.

1. The würde + Infinitive (Most Common) For most verbs, especially in everyday spoken German, you can simply use the conjugated form of werden (would) plus the infinitive verb at the very end of the sentence.

Examples: 

Ich würde gern nach Deutschland reisen. (I would like to travel to Germany.)

Ich würde ein Doppelzimmer bevorzugen. (I would prefer a double room.)
superlative - gern(with pleasure), lieber(rather), am liebsten(most preferably)

Gern: Considered slightly more casual, short, and modern. It is frequently favored in spoken conversation or inside a sentence (e.g., Ich helfe dir gern) simply because it rolls off the tongue quickly.

Gerne: Often sounds slightly more polite, emphasized, or traditional. I
t is very commonly used when answering "You're welcome!" (Gerne geschehen) or when accepting an offer (e.g., Ja, gerne!).

Das klingt gesund und lecker.

Use 'in' for being inside focusing on enclosed spaces(rooms, buildings) or geographical areas (cities, countries). Also for future time spans similarly to English for future time spans (e.g., in einer Stunde - in an hour) and for months, seasons, and periods like in der Nacht. It often contracts with the dative article dem to become "im" (in dem) for months and seasons (e.g., im Sommer - in summer)
Position (Dative Case): Describes being inside something (e.g., Ich bin im (in dem) Kino — I am in the cinema).
Motion (Accusative Case): Describes moving into something (e.g., Ich gehe in den Supermarkt — I am going into the supermarket).
Time: Used for months, years, or future timeframes (e.g., in einer Stunde — in an hour)
An informal, friendly, and highly common way to say "bye," "goodbye," or "cheerio". It is used when leaving a place or parting ways with friends, family, or colleagues.
bald, baldiger, am baldsten

Used primarily to indicate position on top of a horizontal surface, in open spaces/public places, or to express direction/movement. It acts as a two-way preposition: use the dative case for location/stationary position, and the accusative case for movement/destination
On Top of Surfaces: Used when something is resting on a horizontal surface, such as auf dem Tisch (on the table), auf dem Bett (on the bed), or auf dem Boden (on the floor).

Public Places & Open Areas: Used for specific public places, locations, or open areas, such as auf dem Marktplatz (on the market square), auf der Post (at the post office), auf dem Flughafen (at the airport), auf der Straße (on the street), or auf dem Land (in the countryside).
Vertical Surfaces (Sometimes): While an is usually used, auf can be used for things perched on top of vertical areas, such as auf der Mauer (on the wall).
Movement onto a Surface (Accusative): Used to express movement onto something, like Ich lege das Buch auf den Tisch (I lay the book on the table).

Verbs requiring "auf": Several verbs consistently take "auf" (often with accusative), including:
warten auf (to wait for)
freuen auf (to look forward to)
basieren auf (to be based on - takes Dative/Accusative)
bestehen auf (to insist on - takes Dative/Accusative)

Used in the dative case

Used mainly for destinations (cities, countries without articles, "home"), directions (left, right), and time ("after"). It generally means "to" or "after," and always takes the dative case. Common uses include nach Berlin, nach Hause, nach links, and nach der Arbeit.

Geographical Destinations (Without Articles): Used for most cities (nach Berlin), countries (nach Deutschland), and continents (nach Afrika).
Note: Does not apply to countries with articles (e.g., "in die Schweiz").
"Home" (Location): Always nach Hause (going home), not zu Hause (at home).
Directions: Used for compass points and directions: nach Norden (to the north), nach rechts (to the right), nach links (to the left).
Time ("After"): Used to express a later time: nach dem Frühstück (after breakfast), nach 5 Uhr (after 5 o'clock).
Order or Sequence: Indicating someone follows: nach dir (after you).
Nach vs. Zu: Nach is for cities/countries/home; zu is for people (zu Maria) or specific buildings/places (zum Arzt).
Nach vs. In: Nach is used for locations without a specific "inside" implication, whereas in + accusative (in das/ins) implies going into a building or space.
There is a German saying to memorize the prepositions that take the dative: Herr von Nach-Seit-Zu und Frau Aus-Bei-Mit bleiben mit dem Dativ fit.
Always takes the dative
There is a German saying to memorize the prepositions that take the dative: Herr von Nach-Seit-Zu und Frau Aus-Bei-Mit bleiben mit dem Dativ fit.
Translates to 'since' when referring to a starting point in time, or 'for' when referring to a duration of time. It describes an action that started in the past but is still ongoing in present

Seit is a preposition that always triggers the Dative case. You must change the article/pronoun following it.
With a duration of time: seit einem Monat (for a month), seit drei Jahren (for three years).
With a point in time: seit gestern (since yesterday), seit Montag (since Monday).

Seit can also be used as a subordinate conjunction to connect two clauses. In this case, it means "since" (as in "because of the fact that"). The verb in the seit clause is pushed to the very end.
Seit ich in Deutschland lebe, trinke ich viel Kaffee. (Since I live in Germany, I drink a lot of coffee).

Unlike English (which uses the present perfect progressive like "I have been living here for three years"), German uses the simple present tense with seit.
 
Ich wohne seit drei Jahren hier. (I have been living here for three years).
Always takes the dative
There is a German saying to memorize the prepositions that take the dative: Herr von Nach-Seit-Zu und Frau Aus-Bei-Mit bleiben mit dem Dativ fit.
denotes origin (geographical or material), exiting a space (like buildings), or causes/motives (like boredom)

Geographical Origin (From): Used to state where someone is from or where an item originates (countries, cities, regions).
Example: "Ich komme aus der Schweiz." (I come from Switzerland.)

Physical Movement (Out of/From): Indicating moving out of an enclosed space or container.
Example: "Er kommt aus dem Büro." (He is coming out of the office.)
Example: "Ich hole das Buch aus der Tasche." (I'm taking the book out of the bag.)

Cause or Motive (Out of/From): Indicating the reason for an action.
Example: "Ich habe es aus Liebe gemacht." (I did it out of love.)

Material (Made of): Indicating what something is made of.
Example: "Der Tisch ist aus Holz." (The table is made of wood.)

Mit and bei often both translate to "with" in English but have distinct uses: Mit implies accompaniment, tools, or direct involvement ("I walk with him"), while bei denotes location, proximity, or employment
Mit: "Ich gehe mit meiner Freundin ins Kino." (I am going to the movies with my friend - together).
Mit: "Ich schreibe mit einem Stift." (I write with a pen).
Mit: "Ich arbeite mit Lutz." (I work together with Lutz).

It indicates motion (to) or location (at/closed)
It commonly contracts with masculine/neuter articles to zum (zu + dem) or feminine to zur (zu + der)
Direction (to/towards): Ich gehe zum Arzt (m). / Ich fahre zur Arbeit (f).
Location/Fixed Phrases: Zu Hause (at home)
Takes dative case.

Irgendwelche is an indefinite pronoun (Indefinitpronomen) or an indefinite adjective (Indefinitadjektiv) in German. It is used to express that something or someone is unspecified or arbitrary, often translating to "some," "any," or "any kind of" in English
Meaning: It indicates that the speaker doesn't know, doesn't care, or deems it unimportant which particular item or person is referred to.
Usage: It is primarily used with plural nouns or in contexts asking about the existence of multiple things (e.g., Hast du irgendwelche Fragen? — Do you have any questions?).
Declension: Irgendwelche is inflected like the pronoun welche to agree with the grammatical gender and case of the noun it modifies (e.g., irgendwelcher, irgendwelchem).
Distinction: While irgendein is used for singular, unspecified items, irgendwelche is its plural equivalent.

Because wenn creates a subordinate clause, the conjugated verb must go to the very end of that clause.

If the sentence starts with the wenn clause, it occupies the first position. Therefore, the main clause immediately after the comma must start with the verb.

Wenn du Zeit hast, kommst du heute vorbei. (If you have time, come over today.)

If: Used for conditions, possibilities, or hypotheticals.

Wenn es regnet, bleibe ich zu Hause. (If it rains, I stay at home.)

When / Whenever: Used for habitual, recurring events, or future events.

Wenn ich müde bin, gehe ich ins Bett. (When/Whenever I am tired, I go to bed.)

dass (that) is a subordinating conjunction that connects a main clause to a subordinate clause. It is placed immediately after the comma and pushes the conjugated verb to the absolute end of the subordinate sentence.

Example: Ich hoffe, dass du mir helfen kannst.(I hope that you can help me.)

With Auxiliary: Ich denke, dass wir morgen nach Berlin reisen. (I think that we are traveling to Berlin tomorrow.)

When using a separable verb in a dass-clause, the prefix does not separate. The entire verb is kept intact and moved to the end.

 Ich sehe, dass der Zug pünktlich ankommt. (I see that the train arrives on time.)

If you have a modal verb alongside another verb, the modal verb goes to the very end of the dass-clause, behind the infinitive.

Example: Er sagt, dass er das Buch lesen muss. (He says that he must read the book.)

Wahr describes a factual state, statement, or reality that corresponds to the facts (being true),.

(Ehrlich describes an action, a person, or an attitude of openness and lack of deceit (being honest))

"Das ist wahr" (That is true).
"Eine wahre Geschichte" (A true story).

Use damit (so that) when you want to express a goal or aim. The verbs are always in the conjugated form at the end of the sentence.

Ich schreibe die Zutaten auf, damit ich sie nicht vergesse.
I'll write the ingredients down so that I won't forget them.
A subordinate clause with damit can have a different subject from the main clause.
For countable nouns such as Eier(eggs), add an e to the end - wenige Eier
For uncoutable nouns such as Zucker (sugar), use as is - wenig Zucker

Weniger (Comparative form: "Less" / "Fewer")
Meaning "Less" (uncountable nouns):Ich trinke weniger Kaffee. (I drink less coffee.)
Meaning "Fewer" (plural countable nouns):Er hat jetzt weniger Probleme. (He has fewer problems now.)
Like damit, you can also use um … zu to express a goal. However, in this construction, the subject of both clauses is the same, and the verb in the subordinate clause is in the infinitive.

"nimm" is the informal, singular imperative (command) form of the verb nehmen. It directly translates to "take" in English and is used when directly addressing one person you are on a first-name basis with
1. Direct Command / Instruction
Use nimm to tell one person to grab, hold, or accept something.
"Nimm dir einen Stuhl." (Take a chair for yourself.)
"Nimm das nicht persönlich." (Don't take that personally.)

2. Ordering Food or DrinksWhen you are in a restaurant or bakery, you can use nimm (or the slightly more polite nimm doch) to suggest what someone else should get.
"Nimm doch den Kaffee, der ist besser." (Have/Take the coffee, it’s better.)

Trink nicht aus der Flasche, nimm ein Glas!
Don't drink from the bottle, use a glass!
Ich bin klug. (I am smart.)

When used as a subordinating conjunction, während links two clauses and pushes the conjugated verb to the very end of its clause. It typically highlights that two things are happening simultaneously.

Structure: [Main Clause], während [Subordinate Clause ... verb at the end].

Example: Ich lese ein Buch, während er Musik hört. (I read a book while he is listening to music.)
Example: Während du schläfst, koche ich das Abendessen. (While you are sleeping, I am cooking dinner.)

Note: In some cases, während can be used to show contrast, much like the English word "whereas."

Example: Während ich Kaffee mag, trinkt sie lieber Tee. (Whereas/While I like coffee, she prefers to drink tea.)

When used as a preposition, während is followed by a noun instead of a full clause. Grammatically, it requires the Genitive case. However, in casual, spoken German, native speakers often use the Dative case instead.

Structure: während + Noun (Genitive is standard, Dative is colloquial)

Example (Genitive - Formal/Written): Während des Unterrichts dürfen wir nicht sprechen. (During the lesson, we are not allowed to speak.)
Example (Dative - Colloquial/Spoken): Während dem Frühstück lese ich Zeitung. (During breakfast, I read the newspaper.)

Gründend (The Present Participle of Gründen )

This form acts like an adjective or describes an ongoing action, equivalent to the English ending "-ing". It is used when the subject is actively in the process of establishing something right at that moment.

Example usage:
Die gründenden Mitglieder unterschrieben den Vertrag. (The founding/establishing members signed the contract.)

Er saß am Schreibtisch, seine neue Firma gründend. (He sat at his desk, establishing his new company.)

langsam means "slow" or "slowly," while langsamer is the comparative form meaning "slower" or "more slowly."

A simple breakdown of how to use them:

Langsam (Base form): Used to describe a state of low speed.

Example: "Er spricht langsam." (He speaks slowly.)

Langsamer (Comparative form): Used for comparisons or to demand a reduction in speed.

Example: "Er spricht langsamer als sie." (He speaks more slowly than her.)
Imperative: "Langsamer!" or "Sprich langsamer!" (Slower! / Speak more slowly!)

Ich hole die Zutaten aus der Küche.
I'll get the ingredients from the kitchen.

der/die/das nächste ...     - the closest ...

"Ich zahle bar." (I am paying in cash.)

Bezahlen focuses on the specific item, service, or person you are paying for and usually takes a direct (accusative) object.
Example: "Ich bezahle die Rechnung." (I am paying the bill.)
Example: "Ich bezahle das Essen." (I am paying for the food.)

In German, wann translates strictly to "when" when asking about time. It is used for both direct questions and indirect questions. If you can mentally replace "when" with "at what time" or "what time", you should use wann

Direct Questions
Use wann to ask about a specific point in time or duration.
Wann kommt der Zug? (When is the train coming?)V
on wann bis wann bist du im Büro? (From when to when are you at the office?)

Indirect Questions
Use wann when asking or stating time-related information inside a dependent clause.
Ich weiß nicht, wann er kommt. (I don't know when he is coming.)

"um" is most commonly used as a preposition for specific clock times (translating to "at") or as a conjunction in "um... zu" constructions to express purpose (translating to "in order to")

The four primary ways to use "um" include:

Telling Time (Preposition): Use it with clock times. It always takes the Akkusativ case.
Example: um acht Uhr (at eight o'clock)

Expressing Purpose (Conjunction): Use um [verb] zu when the subject in both parts of the sentence remains the same. It translates to "in order to".
Example: Ich lerne Deutsch, um in Deutschland zu arbeiten. (I am learning German in order to work in Germany.)

Surroundings & Measurement (Preposition): Use it to mean "around" a physical location or to indicate a specific change/difference.
Example: Er fährt um die Ecke. (He drives around the corner.)
Example: Der Preis ist um zehn Euro gestiegen. (The price went up by [a margin of] ten euros.)

As a Verb Prefix: "Um-" can be attached to verbs. Depending on the word, it can be an inseparable prefix (e.g., umarmen - to hug) or a separable prefix that changes the word's meaning (e.g., umfahren - to drive around vs. umfahren - to knock over).

1. The Bevor-Clause Comes Last
If you start with the main clause, place bevor, and put the conjugated verb at the very end of the second clause.

Structure: [Main Clause] + , + [bevor] + [Subject/Details] + [Verb].

Example: Ich putze meine Zähne, bevor ich ins Bett gehe. (I brush my teeth before I go to bed.)

2. The Bevor-Clause Comes First
If you start your sentence with bevor, the clause with bevor becomes the first block of your sentence. Because German sentences balance the verb in position two of the overall sentence, the very next thing after the comma must be the conjugated verb of your main clause.

Structure: [bevor] + [Details] + [Verb 1], + [Verb 2] + [Subject/Details].

Example: Bevor du gehst, machst du bitte das Licht aus. (Before you leave, please turn off the light.)

1. The Standard Rule (Genitive Case)
When writing or speaking formally, aufgrund requires the noun following it to be in the genitive.

In German, the preposition anstatt (and its shorter form statt) officially takes the Genitive case. However, in modern colloquial German, it is also frequently used with the Dative case.

1. Genitive Case (Standard/Formal)
When used strictly as a preposition, the noun following anstatt takes the genitive case.

Example: Anstatt des Regens schien die Sonne. (Instead of the rain, the sun shone.)

2. Dative Case (Colloquial/Spoken)In casual everyday speech, many native Germans replace the genitive with the dative case, especially when the genitive article endings are hard to distinguish.

Example: Anstatt dem Regen instead of Anstatt des Regens.

Anstatt can also act as a conjunction (often used with "zu" + infinitive) to connect actions, in which case case rules don't apply to the verb phrase.

Example: Anstatt zu schlafen, habe ich gearbeitet. (Instead of sleeping, I worked.)

Generally requires genitive case.

It is primarily used in formal, written, or business contexts to establish a direct causal connection to an event.

Examples of infolge with the Genitive Case

Masculine: Infolge des Unfalls (As a result of the accident)
Feminine: Infolge der großen Konkurrenz (As a result of the heavy competition)
Neuter: Infolge des starken Regens (As a result of the heavy rain)
Plural: Infolge tagelanger Schneefälle (As a result of days of snowfall)

Key Exceptions & Usage Rules

No Article: If the noun following infolge does not have an article or an adjective to clearly show the genitive case, the dative case is used instead.

The "von" Alternative: 
In spoken or daily German, native speakers often avoid the genitive by using infolge von plus the dative case. Exampe: 

Infolge von tagelangen Schneefällen (As a result of days of snowfall)

Example: "Trotz des schlechten Wetters" (Despite the bad weather).Rule: You add an -s or -es to masculine and neuter nouns, and use der instead of die/das.

Plural without an article: "Trotz Umbaus" (Genitive) vs. "Trotz Umbauten" (Dative).
With pronouns: "Trotz allem" (Despite everything).
In conversational German, using the dative is incredibly common and widely accepted, though purists may consider it sloppy.Example: "Trotz dem schlechten Wetter" (Despite the bad weather).
